q: A certificate for shop.example.com is signed and the padlock shows. What does the certificate prove?
options: That the site is honest and safe
That whoever runs the server controls the name shop.example.com, and holds its private key
That the company behind the site is real
That the app behind the proxy has no bugs
why: A certificate ties a name to a public key, signed by an issuer the browser trusts. It proves control of the name. A phishing site can have a valid certificate for its own name.

q: Put the chain of trust in order, from the certificate your server holds to the one the browser already has.
items: The root certificate in the browser's trust list
why: Each certificate is signed by the next one up. The browser walks up until it reaches a root that is already in its built-in list.

q: Your nginx sends only your own certificate. curl says it cannot get the local issuer certificate. What is the fix?
options: Renew the certificate
Point nginx at fullchain.pem, which also holds the middle certificate
Turn on HSTS
Open port 80
why: The browser or curl must be able to link your certificate to a root. fullchain.pem is your certificate plus the middle ones. cert.pem alone leaves a gap.

q: With TLS termination, the traffic between nginx and your Node app is always encrypted.
why: nginx decrypts the request and makes a new one to the app. That last leg is usually plain HTTP on a private network. To encrypt it too you must re-encrypt, with a certificate on the app.

q: Which of these are true when the proxy ends the HTTPS (terminates TLS)?
options: The certificate and private key live on the proxy
The proxy can read the path and add headers such as X-Forwarded-Proto
The app must hold a certificate too
The app can tell that the visitor used HTTPS only from a header, not from the connection
why: The proxy holds the key and reads the request. The app sees plain HTTP, so it relies on X-Forwarded-Proto. The app needs no certificate in this setup.

q: Cloudflare is in Flexible mode. A visitor sees the padlock. What about the leg from Cloudflare to your server?
options: Encrypted
Not encrypted, it is plain HTTP
Encrypted only if the visitor uses Chrome
Blocked
why: In Flexible mode the visitor leg can be HTTPS but Cloudflare to the origin is not encrypted. Cloudflare recommends Full or Full (strict) when possible.

q: You want one certificate for *.example.com from Let's Encrypt. Port 80 is open. Which challenge must you use?
options: HTTP-01, because port 80 is open
DNS-01, which needs a TXT record and a DNS provider with an API
Either one, it does not matter
Neither, wildcards are not allowed
why: HTTP-01 cannot be used for wildcards. A file on one web server cannot prove control of every name. A TXT record in the DNS can.

q: In the DNS-01 challenge, the tool creates a TXT record. Type the name of the record, which starts with an underscore, for the domain example.com.
why: Let's Encrypt asks for a TXT record at _acme-challenge.<your domain>. HTTP-01 uses a file under /.well-known/acme-challenge/ instead.

q: Which port must be reachable from the internet for the HTTP-01 challenge, even if your site is HTTPS only?
why: The check is plain HTTP on port 80. A firewall change that closes port 80 can break renewal while the site on port 443 still looks fine.

q: Put the longest allowed life of a public certificate in order, from the oldest rule to the newest (the CA/Browser Forum schedule).
why: The industry cuts the longest life in steps: 398, then 200, then 100, then 47 days. The point is to limit damage from a stolen key and to force automation.

q: Let's Encrypt gives 90 day certificates by default. Certbot renews when less than a third of the life is left. How many days before the end does a 90 day certificate become due? Type the number.
why: A third of 90 days is 30 days. With exactly 30 days left it is still ok. One day later it is due.

q: Your cron job renews every 60 days. Let's Encrypt moves you to 45 day certificates. What happens?
options: Nothing, 60 days is fine
The certificate expires before the first renewal
Let's Encrypt renews it for you
The job renews twice as often
why: A fixed 60 day schedule is longer than a 45 day life. Use a tool that checks the real dates (Certbot 4 and later) or asks the CA when to renew with ACME Renewal Information.

q: Let's Encrypt still sends an email when your certificate is close to expiring.
why: Let's Encrypt ended its expiration emails on 2025-06-04. You must monitor days left yourself, or use a monitoring service.

q: Your site sent Strict-Transport-Security with a one year max-age. Today the certificate expired. What does a visitor's browser do?
options: Shows a warning with a Continue anyway button
Shows an error with no way to continue
Ignores the date
Switches to plain HTTP
why: For an HSTS site a browser does not allow click through on a TLS error. A missed renewal becomes a full outage until you fix it. Start HSTS with a short time.
